note: Models validity degrading multiplicatively across pipeline stages, which gives an audit a way to argue a certification claim is overstated.
title: Measurement Without Validity: The Compounding Reliability Problem in Agentic AI Evaluation

reading.body:
A benchmark score is not a capability measurement. It is the product of several stages, each of which loses validity, and the losses multiply.

The paper models evaluation as three layers: task generation, human-simulator calibration, and automated judgment. Total validity is bounded by the product of the three. At 0.70 per stage the ceiling is 0.34, with a reported range of 0.22 to 0.54. The supporting evidence points the same way. Of 55 agentic evaluation papers surveyed, about 82 percent used inter-rater reliability metrics that were mismatched, incomplete, or absent. Task flaws appeared in 7 of 10 benchmarks. Inter-simulator variance reached 9 percentage points.

This matters for AI because benchmark scores are what justify deployment, safety, and compliance decisions. If a pipeline that looks strong at every stage can still be roughly one third valid overall, then a single headline number is not proof of anything. The practical consequence is procedural: stage-by-stage validity evidence and reliability thresholds before a score is accepted, and a documented basis for challenging a certification claim that rests on the score alone.

What the data does not cover is whether the compounding model holds outside agentic evaluation, or how the three layers interact in any specific pipeline. The 0.34 figure is an upper bound under stated assumptions, not a measurement of any named system. The paper is a preprint with zero citations, so the framework has not yet been tested by others. The survey of 55 papers describes reporting practice, not the underlying validity of the evaluations themselves.

explain_beginner: This paper looks at how AI systems are tested before they are trusted with important jobs. The author argues that each testing stage can lose some accuracy, and those losses multiply rather than add up. If three stages each keep 70 percent of their accuracy, the final result may be only about 34 percent trustworthy. The author checked 55 published AI evaluation papers and found most used weak or missing reliability checks. This matters because test scores often justify safety and deployment decisions, and those scores may be far less solid than they appear.
explain_business: This research suggests that AI benchmark scores used for deployment, safety, and compliance may overstate real capability because validity losses compound across evaluation stages. An audit can use this framework to challenge certification claims, since a pipeline strong at each stage can still be only about one third valid overall. The practical decision is to require stage-by-stage validity evidence and reliability thresholds before accepting benchmark results, rather than treating a single score as proof. Leaders should treat evaluation quality as a measurable risk item and demand documentation of task validity, simulator calibration, and judge reliability before signing off.
explain_practitioner: The paper proposes a three-layer model where total validity is bounded by the product of validity at task generation, human-simulator calibration, and automated judgment. With each stage at 0.70, the upper bound is 0.34, with a reported range of 0.22 to 0.54. The author validates this against a survey of 55 agentic evaluation papers, finding about 82 percent used mismatched, incomplete, or absent inter-rater reliability metrics, consistent with judgment-stage collapse. Evidence also includes task flaws in 7 of 10 benchmarks and up to 9 percentage point inter-simulator variance. Eight psychometric prescriptions and stratified ICC and alpha thresholds are provided.
